hints: At M differentiate sec²x√(3+2tanx) with the product and chain rules.
Set the derivative to zero, cancel non-zero common factors, and reduce to an equation in tanx.
Solve on the stated interval, reject endpoint or extraneous candidates, and use the graph's minimum condition to select M's x-coordinate to 3 significant figures.
walkthrough:
Differentiate $y = \sec^2 x\sqrt{3 + 2\tan x}$ using the product rule $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(uv) = u'v + uv'$:
$$u = \sec^2 x = (\sec x)^2 \implies \dfrac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x} = 2\sec x(\sec x\tan x) = 2\sec^2 x\tan x$$
$$v = (3 + 2\tan x)^{1/2} \implies \dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{2}(3 + 2\tan x)^{-1/2}\left(2\sec^2 x\right) = \dfrac{\sec^2 x}{\sqrt{3 + 2\tan x}}$$

Combine into $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$:
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = 2\sec^2 x\tan x\sqrt{3 + 2\tan x} + \dfrac{\sec^4 x}{\sqrt{3 + 2\tan x}}$$

Set $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = 0$ at the stationary point $M$:
$$\dfrac{\sec^2 x}{\sqrt{3 + 2\tan x}}\left[2\tan x(3 + 2\tan x) + \sec^2 x\right] = 0$$
$$\text{Since } \sec^2 x \geqslant 1 > 0 \text{ and } \sqrt{3 + 2\tan x} > 0 \text{ on } \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{4}, \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right):$$
$$2\tan x(3 + 2\tan x) + \sec^2 x = 0$$

Substitute the Pythagorean identity $\sec^2 x = 1 + \tan^2 x$:
$$6\tan x + 4\tan^2 x + (1 + \tan^2 x) = 0$$
$$5\tan^2 x + 6\tan x + 1 = 0$$

Factor the quadratic equation in $\tan x$:
$$(5\tan x + 1)(\tan x + 1) = 0$$
$$\tan x = -1 \quad \text{or} \quad \tan x = -\dfrac{1}{5} = -0.2$$

Select the valid stationary point $M$ inside the interval $-\dfrac{\pi}{4} < x < \dfrac{\pi}{4}$:
$$\tan x = -1 \implies x = -\dfrac{\pi}{4} \quad (\text{boundary endpoint where the curve terminates})$$
$$\tan x = -0.2 \implies x = \tan^{-1}(-0.2) \approx -0.197396 \approx -0.197\text{ rad}$$

ai_rubric.Finding Stationary Points: Differentiates $\sqrt{3+2\tan x}$ to derive $\sec^2x(3+2\tan x)^{-1/2}$; Differentiates $\sec^2x$ to derive $2\sec x\sec x\tan x$; Concludes with $x=-0.197$ (approximately).

hints: With u=3+2tanx, use du=2sec²x dx and change the limits: x=−π/4 gives u=1 and x=π/4 gives u=5.
Integrate (1/2)u^(1/2) between those exact limits and simplify the surds.
walkthrough:
Use the substitution $u = 3 + 2\tan x$:
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x} = 2\sec^2 x \implies \sec^2 x\,\mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{d}u$$

Transform the integration limits:
$$\text{At } x = -\dfrac{\pi}{4}: \quad u = 3 + 2\tan\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = 3 + 2(-1) = 3 - 2 = 1$$
$$\text{At } x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}: \quad u = 3 + 2\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = 3 + 2(1) = 3 + 2 = 5$$

Substitute into the area integral $\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4} \sec^2 x\sqrt{3 + 2\tan x}\,\mathrm{d}x$:
$$\text{Area} = \int_1^5 \sqrt{u}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{d}u\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\int_1^5 u^{1/2}\,\mathrm{d}u$$

Integrate with respect to $u$ using the power rule:
$$\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{u^{3/2}}{3/2}\right]_1^5 = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{2}{3}u^{3/2}\right]_1^5 = \dfrac{1}{3}\left[u^{3/2}\right]_1^5$$

ai_rubric.Integration by Substitution: Gives $du/dx=2\sec^2x$. Reach an integral of the form $\int A\sqrt u\,du$. The final result is $\dfrac{5\sqrt5}{3}-\dfrac13$.
